title: It Turns Out that Knowledge Really Is Power: So, What’s In Your Portfolio?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. opens with the contrast in COVID-19 testing between South Korea and the United States to make a point about learning: when we know little, sophisticated action is impossible, and skill follows knowledge. He cites a Deans for Impact finding that teacher candidates averaged 49 percent on basic cognitive science questions, implying that gaps in professional knowledge limit teaching quality. After naming system-level implications such as knowledge-rich PD and curricula, he turns to what teachers control, their own knowledge portfolios. Borrowing the idea from The Pragmatic Programmer, he argues that teachers should invest in learning regularly and as a habit, like managing a financial portfolio. The piece is a call for teachers to take ownership of their professional learning.
points: Skill follows knowledge, for governments and for teachers alike.
Teacher candidates averaged 49 percent on basic cognitive science principles, which suggests a real gap in professional knowledge.
Systemic fixes include knowledge-rich PD, coherent curricula, and assessments that reveal both skill and knowledge.
Teachers can manage a personal knowledge portfolio by investing regularly and habitually in their own learning.
quotes: My point isn’t politics. It’s that governments, it turns out, have one of the same limitations that human beings do: when we don’t know enough, sophisticated action is not possible; when we know more, our abilities improve.
Skill follows knowledge. This is a fundamental truth of learning. When you know more, you’re able to argue better, think better, and learn more things better.

According to a recent report by Deans for Impact, when 1,000 teacher candidates from a handful of teacher colleges were quizzed on basic principles of cognitive science in the fall of 2019, their average percentage score was 49%. It wasn’t a measurement of the teachers’ skills — just a measurement of their knowledge.

There are all sorts of implications for our work here — the need for knowledge-rich, evidence-informed PD; the need for coherent, sequential, cumulative, knowledge-rich curricula at every grade level; the need for classroom-based assessments that teach us both what our students can do (skill) and what our students know.

We like to think of all the facts programmers know about computing, the application domains they work in, and all their experience as their Knowledge Portfolios. Managing a knowledge portfolio is very similar to managing a financial portfolio.

Almost all of us are experiencing a wider-than-normal gap between what we’d like to be able to do for our students and what we’re actually able to do. There’s perhaps never been a better time to assess the balance of our knowledge portfolios and invest accordingly.
